newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Lockheed offers Czechs F-16s for $24 mln.
newsitem.headline: Lockheed offers Czechs F-16s for $24 mln.

text.p: Lockheed Martin Corp, on Wednesday launched its first volley in a post-Cold War bidding battle to supply the Czechs with a fleet of advanced fighter aircraft, offering its flagship F-16s for $24 million apiece.
"We offer F-16's ... for 30 percent less than the nearest competitor," Dain Hancock, president of Lockheed's tactical aircraft systems, told a news conference.
Later he specified that the price for "a brand new fighter would be $24 million each." The Czechs are looking to upgrade their fleet of 24 ageing Soviet-made Mig-21 aircraft.
Hancock said if the Czechs chose the F-16, they would have to allow for two to three years for first delivery.
The Czechs along with former Warsaw Pact allies Poland and Hungary, all seen as front-runners to join NATO, and need to modernise their fleets to be compatible with the military alliance.

Czech defence officials have said they have the will but not the wallet to buy brand new western-made advanced fighters, but are keeping their options open as a battle over the long-term military budget goes on.

Lockheed Martin is competing for post-Cold War business in central Europe against U.S. McDonnell Douglas, maker of the F/A-18 "Hornet", Sweden's SAAB, which makes the "Gripen", France's "Mirage" and other European builders.
To strengthen its bid with the Czechs, Hancock said Lockheed has contacted about 40 Czech industrial companies offering possible cooperation, a method also announced by McDonnell Douglas.
These companies include aeroplane producers like Aero Vodochody, Let Kunovice, Letov Praha or weapons trading companies like Omnipol, and Skoda Plzen.
Details of what this cooperation would entail were not disclosed.
However, the Czech government has been delaying a decision on buying any aircraft as proposed cuts in defence spending have clouded the debate over the upgrading of the fleet.
The Czech military has said it would need about 24 fighters to replace its old MiG-21s, while Hungary said it needs around 30 and Poland 100.
Analysts say the planes typically cost over $20 million a piece new without supplementary equipment and technology. A cheaper option would be to buy second-hand planes at a fraction of the cost.
Hancock said any deal on used fighters would have to come through an agreement between the U.S. government and Czech authorities.
